title: How I got into Stocks
content: Back in 2020, during COVID outbreak, I saw plane travel demand drop drastically. Nasdaq recorded an extreme fall of 30% in March 2020 with VIX spiking to 85. I knew this was a chance to buy airplane company stocks, and in fact, all stocks. But I have just entered high school and I did not have a stock account. Years later, after I graduated high school, I came to see that it was indeed a crazy opportunity to buy the dip. With mad regrets about missing a once in a 10 year opportunity, I started studying stocks.

The first ever stock that I purchased after studying the basics was 035720 (Kakao Corp.) in KOSPI (Korean Stock Exchange) around 2022. But I haven't realized that KOSPI is ass and it moves either horizontally or in circles. I think I bought ~$1000 just to record -10% after 2 years and I got demotivated and stopped doing stocks for a while (actually it's still negative as of 2026 if I kept it lol). It only got more serious during my later years of college, when I started realizing that wealth can only be achieved with either: start-up, franchise, or investment, and I have no option other than investment, so I better start being good at investing from my early age.

As of now, after outperforming Nasdaq for quite some time, (about XXX% more than NQ / per year) it seems like I'm starting to understand the stock market a bit. But it's still hard. Lately, I have been analyzing the market geometry and decoding the math behind the market more than doing ordinary company research. I'll talk about this more on a different post.

In Grinnell College, I met cool people who are managing half-million to millions and shared ideas on investments (and I persuaded one of them to invest in HIMS, which dropped 70% after their purchase lol). It seems like this college has a lot of people interested in stocks. I'm currently transferring to Columbia University to study Operations Research, basically math – Stochastic Calculus, Optimization, Markov Chains, Brownian Motions, etc – and hopefully I encounter motivating people with shared interests during my journey there.

title: Dalio's Principles and Reflection on Risks in Life
content: Risk is rather an important concept, not only in stocks, but in life. When we take risk on an event with uncertain probability it's a 'gamble'. Since everything is uncertain in life, life is a gamble. There are different ways to make this gamble favorable. We can either 1. minimize the risk (increase the win rate or minimize the penalty at loss) or 2. bet on an event with high return/loss ratio (i.e. if you win, you win big and if you fail you lose very little). Sadly, risk and R/L ratio are usually proportional by nature; events with high return/loss ratio have high risk (take start-up, for instance), and events with low R/L ratio have low risk (e.g. working at Starbucks). Events with high R/L ratio and low risk are hard to achieve in essence (e.g. becoming a doctor), and events with high risk and low R/L ratio are hedonistic or events you end up through emotion based decisions. Anyways, learning risks can drastically change the probability distribution over paths of your life.

Lately, I realized my risk decisions are inconsistent, not grounded on certain principle or reason, but mostly volatile and grounded on emotions and 'gut feeling'. As a result, I have randomized my probability distribution and left it to God's coin toss. So I took some time to reflect my past judgments and how I want my risk profile to be.

Ray Dalio's book 'Principles' talks about risk managing in life as well. However I found his claims rather a common sense or tautology in most of the parts about risk. But we agree on the common starting point: building a risk profile starts with figuring out the Goal first and asking 'What am I actually optimizing for?' Then, we can aim for different profiles: high risk high reward, low risk high reward, low risk low reward, etc. Now, here are some principles I'vebuilt over time:

1. Never choose high risk + low R/L ratio events. These are choices that either people 'end up making' due to circumstances/emotions or are pleasure based choices. A lot of times, false sense of risk may come from information asymmetry; hence, one way is to avoid taking an event that you consider of this category is to gather the most information about this event.

2. Conditions for going 'all in' (high risk, high reward event). 1.1: For going all in, ensure you have more chances or some safety margin. For example, at young age, you can go all in for a start-up since age is your safe margin. 1.2: Set a stop loss. The best traders in the market are magicians of stop loss; and the best stop loss is placed at a point that invalidates your initial reason of the entry. I personally think this is gold reference to risk in life. Do not stick around with failed positions because your ego holds it. Rather, withdraw from the event if some combination of circumstances (i.e. the loss) invalidates the choice of event. This stop loss is not set after you start the event, due to fear or emotion. It should mostly be set before you start engaging in the event when you are setting the goal. For example, I close this business if it can't reach XX in sales by next year. I stop re-taking college entrance exams if I can't score higher than YY. However, these stop loss conditions should be carefully chosen to prevent false negatives (false invalidations). 1.3 Failure in going all in for that event should open doors to more things (connecting the dots). For example, at least you might get experience while doing that event, that serves for future events.

3. Be consistent with your risk profile. If you choose all in, it's all in. If you choose safe play, it's safe play by minimizing the risk at all times. You can never switch based on emotion or gut feeling.
4. Decrease the risk. For any event, there are ways to decrease the risk: having, a priori, more information about it.
